The '''1668 Ayuman Cup''', recognised retrospectively as the 3rd edition of the '''[[FLLA World Cup]]''', was an international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the leading Ayuman football associations. It was held in [[Eldjo]], across [[Ayuma]], from 4 June to 2 July 1668, and was won by [[Lycroa]], who defeated [[Estijan]] 2–1 in the [[#Final|final]] at the Jioquin Grand Stadium to claim their second title, following their win at the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660 edition]].<ref name="heritage-overview">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/overview|title=The 1668 Ayuman Cup: tournament overview|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 May 1763}}</ref>

The tournament resumed the competition after the cancellation of the [[1664 FLLA World Cup|1664 edition]], which had been abandoned because of the [[Great Imperial War]]; the eight-year interval between the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660]] and 1668 editions was the longest gap in the contest's history to that point. It was staged under the older title of the Ayuman Cup, the name the competition bore before the [[FLLA]] was constituted and the contest was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]]; the seven continental confederations did not yet exist, and all twelve entrants were drawn from [[Ayuma]].<ref name="heritage-rename">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/history/early-competition-names|title=From the Ayuman Cup to the FLLA World Cup: the early names of the competition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1764}}</ref>

The 1668 edition was the first to be contested for the original rotating '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]]''', the cast-bronze trophy commissioned for this edition to replace the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] that had been awarded at the first two tournaments. It was presented to the victorious Lycroan side at the close of the final. The original Andah Cup continued to be contested at every edition until it was lost in [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]] in 1688; the bespoke permanent-trophy tradition that came to characterise the competition began only with the relaunch at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]].<ref name="heritage-trophy">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-andah-cup|title=The original Andah Cup, introduced in 1668, and its loss in 1688|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

==Host selection==

The 1668 tournament was awarded to [[Eldjo]] by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal body that organised the competition before the foundation of the [[FLLA]]. With the competition having lain dormant since the abandonment of the [[1664 FLLA World Cup|1664 edition]], the award to Eldjo was framed as a means of restarting the contest in a settled part of [[Ayuma]] once the [[Great Imperial War]] had subsided. The Eldjon organisers undertook to stage the finals across five cities, with the principal matches held in the capital, [[Jioquin]].<ref name="heritage-host">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/host|title=1668 Ayuman Cup: the award of hosting rights to Eldjo|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 May 1763}}</ref>

==Format==

The 12 entered teams were divided into three groups of four for the group stage. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing the other three sides in its group; two points were awarded for a win and one for a draw, in line with the scoring system then in use. The three group winners advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] directly, and were joined by the best of the three group runners-up, determined first by points, then by goal difference and then by goals scored. Where teams within a group finished level on points, places were determined first by goal difference and then by goals scored.

The knockout stage consisted of two semi-finals, a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] and a final, each played as a single-elimination tie over 90 minutes. A tie level at the end of normal time was extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; under the regulations of the period, any tie still level after extra time was to be settled by a replay rather than by a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]], a procedure not yet in use. No replay proved necessary in 1668. The two losing semi-finalists contested the third-place playoff on the day before the final.

==Participating teams==

Twelve teams took part in the 1668 finals, all of them Ayuman national associations. The continental confederations that later structured the [[FLLA World Cup]] had not yet been established, and qualification was settled under the informal arrangements of the period; as host nation, [[Eldjo]] took part automatically. The participating teams were:<ref name="heritage-teams">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/teams|title=1668 Ayuman Cup: participating teams|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=21 May 1763}}</ref>

==Venues==

Five stadiums in five host cities, all in [[Eldjo]], were used in the final tournament. The principal venue was the Jioquin Grand Stadium in the capital, [[Jioquin]], which staged the opening match and the final and was the largest ground in use. The two semi-finals were divided between the Shorakim Arena in [[Shorakim]] and the Suveto Stadium in [[Suveto]], with the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] held at Velsar Park in [[Velsar]]. The remaining group-stage fixtures were shared between these grounds and the smallest venue, at [[Xaipla]].<ref name="heritage-venues">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/venues|title=Host stadiums of the 1668 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=21 May 1763}}</ref>

==Squads==

Each participating association registered a squad of eighteen players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers; the smaller squads of the period reflected the limited substitution rules then in force, under which a single replacement was permitted only for an injured goalkeeper. A total of 216 players were registered for the tournament.<ref name="heritage-squads">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/squads|title=1668 Ayuman Cup: registered squads|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=21 May 1763}}</ref>

==Match officials==

The organising congress appointed a panel of referees and linesmen drawn from the associations not represented in the latter stages of the competition. The opening match was refereed by Korin Vash of [[Verusa]], and the final by Aldric Venn of [[Darewa]], the senior official of the tournament. The small officiating pool of the period meant that several referees took charge of fixtures involving teams from neighbouring associations, though never from their own.<ref name="heritage-officials">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/officials|title=Match officials of the 1668 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=21 May 1763}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The three groups were each contested as a single round-robin. The winner of each group advanced to the knockout stage, together with the best of the three runners-up; points were awarded on the two-points-for-a-win system in use at the time, with goal difference and then goals scored used to separate teams level on points.

All dates are given in the local time of the host cities.

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the three group winners and the best runner-up. The draw was arranged so that the host, [[Eldjo]], met the [[Group A]] winner, [[Estijan]], in one semi-final, while the other two group winners, [[Lycroa]] and [[Siana]], met in the second. Ties level after 90 minutes were to be extended by a single period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; no tie in 1668 required extra time or a replay.

===Final===

The final was held at the Jioquin Grand Stadium on 2 July 1668 before an estimated crowd of 18,000. [[Estijan]] led at the interval through Brod Halson, but [[Lycroa]] recovered after the break: Tomas Calier, the tournament's leading scorer, levelled the tie before Ferid Voral struck the winner late on for a 2–1 victory. The win secured Lycroa's first title, and the original [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]] was presented to the Lycroan captain at the close of the match.<ref name="heritage-final">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/final|title=The 1668 Ayuman Cup final: Lycroa 2–1 Estijan|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 May 1763}}</ref>

==Statistics==

===Goalscorers===

A total of 52 goals were scored in 22 matches, an average of 2.36 per match. The leading scorer was the Lycroan forward Tomas Calier, who scored six goals across the tournament, including one in the final. No formal individual awards were presented at the 1668 edition: the leading-player, top-scorer and best-goalkeeper prizes (the [[FLLA World Cup#Awards|Vairan Ball, Marskval and Bastion]]) were not instituted until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], and the figures below are recognised retrospectively in the [[FLLA]]'s heritage records.<ref name="heritage-stats">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1668/statistics|title=1668 Ayuman Cup statistical record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=21 May 1763}}</ref>

==Trophy and significance==

The 1668 edition holds a place in the history of the [[FLLA World Cup]] as the tournament that revived the competition after the abandonment of the [[1664 FLLA World Cup|1664 edition]] in the [[Great Imperial War]]. It was the first of the early editions to be decided by a knockout stage built around a best-runner-up place, a device the organising congress adopted to give the twelve-team field a four-team semi-final round. Lycroa's victory was their second major title, following their win at the [[1660 FLLA World Cup|1660 edition]], and confirmed the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] association as one of the leading sides of the early Ayuman game.<ref name="heritage-overview" />

The cup that Lycroa lifted was the original rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], introduced at the 1668 edition to replace the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] of the first two tournaments. The new trophy continued to rotate among the champions until it was lost at the outbreak of the [[Red War]] in 1688; when the competition was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], the host association commissioned a bespoke permanent trophy instead, beginning the permanent-trophy tradition that has characterised the competition ever since.<ref name="heritage-trophy" />
